title: Harris warns Democrats a third Trump impeachment is a waste of time - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
Kamala Harris is telling Democrats not to chase a third Trump impeachment if they retake the House, citing scarce resources and a Senate that will not convict.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris used a midterm-week interview to steer her party away from another high-stakes showdown with President Trump. Speaking with MeidasTouch’s Aaron Parnas, she said Democrats should put limited energy into investigations and accountability instead of a process she already knows will fail in the Senate.
The Hill reported her blunt assessment Tuesday as Republicans and Democrats trade predictions about what happens if the House flips next week. Harris framed impeachment as a dead end. She wants the party focused on governing after the election, not another doomed trial.
Her message lands as House Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans insist Democrats are already primed to move. It also collides with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries keeping every option open. The former vice president is effectively asking her side to stop treating impeachment as the default response.
Harris says the votes are not there and never were
Harris did not hedge. She told Parnas the direction of impeachment is a mistake.
“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you,”
She tied the judgment to hard limits on time and money, and to her own experience sitting through the last Senate trial.
“Just because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations.”
Then she drove the point home on the numbers.
“Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-around, and the votes aren’t there. So, that’s how I feel. But also, I think after the election, we all have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done.”
Just the News noted she also wants Democrats uncompromising on healthcare cuts and oversight of the Iran war. Accountability and investigations, in her telling, are the proper tools. A third impeachment is not.
That stance is more cautious than some in her party have floated. Democrats have not ruled out a fresh attempt if they win the House. They have also left open the chance of targeting Cabinet officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Harris is drawing a brighter line than the rank and file.
Prior trials already proved the Senate math
Trump remains the only U.S. president impeached twice. Both efforts ended in acquittal. Democrats first impeached him in late 2019 over accusations tied to Ukraine and then-former Vice President Joe Biden. The Senate cleared him in February 2020 on 48-52 and 47-53 votes.
The second round came in 2021 over the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, just days after Harris took the oath as vice president. The Senate voted 57-43 to acquit. Every Democrat backed conviction. Seven Republicans joined them. That still fell well short of the 67 votes required.
History offers little comfort to anyone counting on removal. Andrew Johnson’s 1868 trial ended in acquittal. Bill Clinton’s 1999 trial did the same. Richard Nixon faced a likely House impeachment before he resigned in 1974. Harris lived through the most recent failure and is telling colleagues the outcome will not change.
Her warning also tracks with earlier Democratic divisions over forced floor votes, including when Al Green forced another Trump impeachment vote and accused colleagues of shielding the president.
Jeffries keeps the door cracked while Johnson predicts day one
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has refused to take impeachment off the table. Speaking to ABC News last month, he offered a process answer rather than a hard no.
“We’ve got to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution, and then let the chips fall where they may, in the best interests of the American people,”
That is the language of a leader who will not restrain the conference. It leaves room for articles if Democrats believe the facts support them. Harris is arguing the opposite: the facts of Senate arithmetic already decide the question.
Speaker Mike Johnson sounded certain the other way. In a Tuesday interview with pro-Trump pundit Scott Jennings, Johnson said Democrats would move almost immediately if they take power.
“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day, first or second day,”
He added that articles have already been filed in this Congress and that Democrats are “raring to go.” Republican leaders have insisted for months that a Democratic House means another impeachment push next year. Johnson’s comments fit that drumbeat.
Those warnings sit alongside earlier filings, including when Al Green filed yet another impeachment resolution against the president this term.
Clinton calls it a sideshow; Republicans brace for probes
The New York Post reported that Hillary Clinton has staked out similar ground. She opposed impeaching Trump as a sideshow that cannot produce a conviction, while still favoring investigations of officials such as Hegseth. The former secretary of state and the former vice president are both telling Democrats the removal path is closed.
That leaves investigations as the preferred pressure campaign. Harris wants resources aimed there. Clinton wants the same. Jeffries will not rule anything out. The gap between “investigations” and “impeachment” is where the party’s post-election fight will land if the House flips.
Fox News highlighted the same core advice from Harris as Democrats weigh control of Congress. The practical effect is a public split: some voices want another floor spectacle, while senior figures call it a resource sink with no conviction at the end.
Trump has already signaled he will not absorb another round quietly. He has warned he could answer a third attempt by opening probes of his own, a posture laid out when Trump warned he could probe Clinton, Obama and Biden if Democrats try again.
Midterms will test whether Democrats listen
Next week’s elections will decide whether Harris’s advice even matters. If Republicans hold the House, the question stays theoretical. If Democrats win, the conference will have to choose between her counsel and the louder calls for articles on day one.
She is asking them to treat the Senate’s two prior acquittals as final. She is asking them to spend political capital on investigations rather than a third trial that cannot remove the president. And she is asking them to shift from confrontation theater to “get stuff done” once the votes are counted.
Whether that lands with a caucus that has already filed articles and left every option open is another matter. The record shows two impeachments, two acquittals, and a former vice president who sat through the last one telling her party to stop.
Democrats can chase another failed removal, or they can take the counsel of someone who already watched the votes fall short. Voters will soon learn which impulse wins.
